problem: Which of the following gives the line integral of the function $f(x,y)=x\,{e}^{1-{y}^{2}}$ along the quarter-circle ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}=36,$ traversed from the point $(6,0)$ to the point $(0,6)$ in the first quadrant?
worked_solution:
We will use the formula

$$
{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}s={\int }_{a}^{b}f(r(t))\,‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t.
$$

 

The curve $C$ is a part-circle of radius $6$ centered at $O,$ shown below. 

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14057418/assets/c1e3332017b795ed6733a0547e6e449fdba3874f1d1e755118a0687ccaf7448c.png)

The curve $C$ can be parametrized as 

$$
r(t)=⟨6\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,6\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩,\,0\le t\le \frac{\pi }{2}.
$$

Computing ${r}^{′}(t)$ and $‖{r}^{′}(t)‖,$ we get following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(6\operatorname{cos}⁡t)i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(6\operatorname{sin}⁡t)j \\  & =-6\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+6\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j \\ ‖{r}^{′}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{(-6\operatorname{sin}⁡t)^{2}+(6\operatorname{cos}⁡t)^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{36{sin}^{2}⁡t+36{cos}^{2}⁡t} \\  & =\sqrt{36({sin}^{2}⁡t+{cos}^{2}⁡t)} \\  & =6\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $f(x,y)=x\,{e}^{1-{y}^{2}},$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(t)) & =6\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,{e}^{1-(6\operatorname{sin}⁡t)^{2}} \\  & =6\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,{e}^{1-36{sin}^{2}⁡t}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write the integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}{e}^{x+y}\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}f(r(t))\,‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}6\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,{e}^{1-36{sin}^{2}⁡t}\cdot 6\cdot \text{d}t \\  & =36{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,{e}^{1-36{sin}^{2}⁡t}\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$
